newsitem.title: USA: White House disappointed by line-item veto ruling.
newsitem.headline: White House disappointed by line-item veto ruling.

text.p: The White House expressed disappointment on Friday over a court ruling overturning a law that strongly expanded presidential veto power, and the Justice Department considered a quick Supreme Court appeal.

Spokesman Mike McCurry said the White House legal counsel's office was considering what steps can be taken after a judge declared unconstitutional the new "line-item veto" law. It gives President Bill Clinton and his successors the power to quash individual spending items from the U.S. budget.

Presidents of both parties had long coveted such power because it vastly expands their room for manoeuvre in budgetary matters and enables them to prune spending bills to their taste without vetoing an entire bill passed by Congress. Traditionally, all-or-nothing had been their only recourse.
The Republican-led Congress approved the new privilege in March 1996 and Clinton, a Democrat, was the first president to benefit -- although he had not yet used it.

But six dissenting members of Congress filed suit claiming the law violated the processes laid out by the Constitution for making or changing a law, and U.S. District Judge Thomas Jackson sided with them in his ruling on Thursday.
"We are disappointed and we're studying the (court) opinion," McCurry said. "The president fully intended to use the line-item veto when necessary to protect the interests of U.S. taxpayers."

A senior official at the Justice Department, which had defended the law, said an appeal to the Supreme Court was "virtually a foregone conclusion," but added that it remained to be decided just how quickly to proceed.

The law includes a provision that allows the losing side in a court challenge to go directly to the Supreme Court. Legal experts have long expected that the nine high court justices ultimately would have the final word on the law's constitutionality.

Under the court's normal schedule, the justices would hear arguments in the term that begins in October. But the court in rare instances involving exceptionally important cases can speed up arguments so a decision could be reached by July.
After consultations with the White House, a Justice Department official said he hoped for a decision later on Friday on whether to seek high court arguments before the summer recess.

The line-item veto law, which expires in eight years unless extended, took effect in January. Although a Democrat stood to reap the initial benefit, the reform was a key element of the conservative "Contract with America" agenda of the Republican Congress.

But Judge Jackson said in a 36-page ruling that the law "hands off to the president authority over fundamental legislative choices" in conflict with the separation of powers sought by America's Founding Fathers, and spares Congress from making "vexing choices" over which programmes to cut."
"It will take a little bit of time to review what the judge did," one Justice Department lawyer said. "We will look very carefully at this."
Under the law, the president can sign a spending bill and within five days cancel specific items, including appropriations, tax breaks covering 100 or fewer people and new or expanded entitlements.

Congress still has final say. A line-item veto can be overridden by a two-thirds majority in each chamber, just as in the case of normal vetoes. Forty-three of the 50 state governors have line-item veto power over their legislatures.
